texto: genuinely an insultingly bad movie. the most bizarre thing in this movie is what i would argue is the most important part of any art piece, it’s messaging. the majority of this is done through characters and how their path or them “floating on the breeze” as the movie bullshittingly puts it ends for them. people only consistently get good endings if they do what they are told to do and subscribe to the very societal tendencies that led many of them to their hardships. in lieutenant dan’s case, he’s finally happy when he literally converts to christianity and does the capitalistic stereotype of pulling himself up by his bootstraps. need i mention that he does this by coming into an accidental windfall (posed by the movie as a strength of character) in a majority black business. this means that he literally monopolizes a black industry and that’s how he finds happiness. colonizing the fucking shrimp industry. also, the system of capitalism is what led him to the despair because ya know… vietnam. shouldn’t have to spell that out for you. speaking of vietnam the movie also chickenshits out about criticizing any part of american history and usually treats most of the countries faults that are present in the film as a joke. jenny also falls victim to incredibly shitty and misogynistic messaging, perhaps being the worst offender. as a victim of childhood sexual abuse, she obviously HAS to fulfill the cliche and become a sex worker! that’s how it works guys! and of course she’s only happy and only finds meaning in being a mother and forrest’s wife. how fucking cool is that? similarly, throughout the movie she is punished for criticizing the nation as that’s when she falls in with uncouth men (side note: she’s defined by men the entire fucking movie) who treat her wrong and are dirty communists. it’s only when she accepts her place as a woman and stops thinking critically that she becomes happy. but oh no, you can’t move on from your mistakes! especially if you are a woman who’s been sleeping around because obviously the only ending for her is to die of aids. so through jenny, the movie states that women are 1) defined by men, 2) must be faithful to a “good” man (like forrest) and 3) will be punished and are morally wrong for being independent. very cool. now let’s talk about forrest. who is largely who the movie depicts as the ideal american. he never once questions what he’s being told go do and is endlessly rewarded for it. spoiler alert, this is not a great message to send especially considering you know VIETNAM. that messaging is genuinely just brutally disrespectful to the victims of the vietnam war and atrocities like the my lai massacre. as for other issues, the movie is just nostalgia slop. it’s basically the ready player one of american history. shit is just shoehorned in to the point of being corny and to the point of becoming obvious glorification of america while glazing over it’s faults. the constant and egregious needle drops also really turbo suck and start to feel similar to the historical “references” where they are just purposeless. the most atrocious of these is setting a scene of attempted suicide to fucking FREE BIRD BY LYNYRD SKYNYRD. that should honestly be all i have to say about this dogshit movie. perhaps the main thing i took away from this movie is an insight into one of the main reasons that media literacy is dead today. much like the movie wants you to do, many people are simply told forrest gump is good and therefore watch it expecting it to be good and refuse to view it with a critical eye. this causes people to look over it’s genuinely disgusting messaging and handling of historical events and chalk it up to be a good movie because other people like it. genuinely fuck this movie. if you like it i have no respect for you as a person and you are the exact kind of disgusting  sherson (sheep person) that this stupid fucking movie glorifies.

Forrest Gump, a mi parecer, es un filme de propaganda conservadora . Nos muestran cómo a Forrest, que obedece y no cuestiona nada, le va mejor en la vida. Mientras que Jenny, una mujer rebelde que defiende sus ideas y participa en protestas, termina muriendo habiendo pasado por mucho sufrimiento y tragedias. Si pudiera resumir esta película en una frase, sería: " Si obedeces al sistema, te premia; si te rebelas, te castiga ". Así que no es una película bonita de un hombre con discapacidad intelectual de buen corazón. Esa descripción del personaje se usa para demostrar que, a pesar de las dificultades individuales, podemos superarnos y lograr cosas realmente importantes. Lo cual no es un mensaje malo, pero en la película Forrest no realiza un cuestionamiento moral de su participación en la guerra de Vietnam; solo nos muestran que recibe un premio por sus hazañas, pero no hay una reflexión de lo que la guerra significó y si ese premio era en verdad algo de lo que debía estar orgulloso de recibir.

I want to preface this by saying that I still enjoyed this movie and am also willing to admit that maybe I misinterpreted it but here are my thoughts. I don't usually write long reviews, but for this one I'm willing to make an exception. To me, Forrest Gump is a seriously bad movie that only gets worse with time. Whether its creators intended it this way or not, this film preaches conservatism in its bones. It celebrates family values and obedience to the system over anyone who clashes with it, while any morsel of the concept rebellion is scrutinised. To quote someone else: "This no-nothing white man becomes a war hero and a wealthy man simply by chugging along, participating in a country that dictates his every move. He never comprehends racism or the complexities of Vietnam; the movie portrays political activism and hippy culture as a giant cartoon beyond Forrest’s understanding, while presenting his apolitical stance as the height of all virtue. Viewed in retrospect, Forrest Gump whitewashes and dumbs down American history at every turn. " But that's just my two cents.

I remember finding the novel Forrest Gump at the public library a few years before the film came out, based on a recommendation from a family member. It was a slight but breezily enjoyable read. The cover is what I remember best. A man's head, upright in portrait mode, but the facial features themselves were turned 90 degrees. It sounds creepy but it came off as more comedic, which fit the tone of a book about a guy who just seemed to drift from historical event to historical event. A few years later the film became a massive cultural phenomenon, and it was no longer difficult to find the novel in bookstores. It was everywhere, now emblazoned with Tom Hanks . The film itself followed basically the same plot, from what I remembered, but sanded off some of the edges of the titular character. In the book Gump at least experiments with drugs and if I'm not totally mistaken engages in more serious crimes. I remember being disappointed in the film relative to the book, and confounded by its huge success. In retrospect, its success seems now unremarkable. Gump came along at exactly the right time to be supercharged by boomer nostalgia. The film follows Forrest from childhood to adulthood, a man who overcomes his low IQ to achieve great heights as a college football star, a war hero, and a businessman, among other accomplishments. Unlike the film Being There , where a similarly improbable rise is used for satirical effect, director Robert Zemeckis aims for more of a light procession through the historical touchstones and social changes of the 1950s to 1980s. Hanks does an excellent job with the character, even if his performance became so quoted and parodied as to almost mask his actual film performance. He makes it easy to believe that beneath Forrest's apparent innocence and genial attitude toward life is a wandering soul, and a man capable of anger, love, and the entire range of adult emotions. The film crowned Zemeckis as the king of cinematic boomer nostalgia, nine years after he transported a Gen X teenager to the 1950s in Back to the Future . It's hard to see if he meant the film to be anything more than light boomer entertainment. It's so easy to read meaning into Forrest's passage through life that many found him to be inspirational, even as a religious figure, though this seems like overreach. The real underlying theme, intentional or not, is in the way the darker trends of each historical era drags down the weaker characters. It's been noted by others than the character arc of Forrest's lifelong dream girl Jenny ( Robin Wright ) is something of a dark echo of Forrest's journey. As Forrest hops from one wholesome American activity to the next, Jenny weaves her way through the counterculture of the 1960s and onward, and suffers for it. A conservative wet dream of moral judgement is rendered upon her, divine punishment for a wanton, hedonistic lifestyle. It's something of a break from the source novel and from the overall breezy tone of the film, which makes it seem a deliberate thematic choice. All of this makes for a film that draws a wide range of opinions. For me, the film is undeniably well made and acted, but is a little too openly targeted at stroking the id of my parents' generation, as can be seen in the too-cute-by-half opening quote above. I generally prefer films that are the product of their bygone era to those that are a merely a paean to one. Add in its reactionary politics, and my annoyance as a high schooler when Gump beat out the far superior Pulp Fiction for the Best Picture Oscar, and my opinion is a bit low. This may be a good film that nonetheless isn't a film for me. At least Hanks had the good sense to turn down what I assume was tens of millions of dollars on offer to reprise his role in a sequel.

This is perhaps most apparent in Jenny’s misogynistic narrative, in which a woman is repeatedly punished for experiencing trauma, villainised for attempting to reclaim the autonomy that was taken from her, and ultimately expected to reward the affections of a man who spends much of the film pressuring her, guilting her and reminding her of her trauma. I’m not gonna lie this movie is iconic there’s something captivating about it it almost feels subliminal. as a kid I loved Forrest Gump but I got older and and learned the historical realities of the time period this movie takes place in. Now to me this movie was fundamentally misguided it’s attempt to rewrite the narrative of the US involvement in the Vietnamese Civil War is actually disgusting and implications of Forrest time in Vietnam are present throughout the entirety of the film.  Knowing that the creators of this film went to the Pentagon to try to get funding, just makes this feel like a green berets level psyop of a movie. Obviously Green Berets actually got the funding and was rewritten by the US military to serve its own purposes, but you can just tell in this movie that they were trying so hard to get that investment. Boot, licking slop I can’t even drive past a Bubba Gump Shrimp now without getting a little sad that one of my favorite movies as a kid was this morally bankrupt.

Forrest Gump is the most overrated Best Picture winner of its era, and watching it again only deepens the insult. The director doesn't tell a story so much as assemble a highlight reel of the 20th century, then hand the remote to a man who was never in the room. Forrest stumbles through Vietnam, Watergate, and the civil rights movement without understanding a single one of them — and the film treats his blankness as wisdom. The message, stripped of its chocolate-box charm, is pure reactionary fantasy: if you obey, don't question, and never think, America will reward you. Run across the country and you'll get a following. Invest in a shrimp boat and you'll get a fortune. It's fortune-cookie philosophy dressed as profundity. But the real crime is Jenny. Presented as Forrest's great love, she is written as a human wrecking ball — she uses him, abandons him, reappears when it suits her, and drags him into her chaos at every turn. The film asks us to pity her, yet she's the one character who sees Forrest clearly and treats him worst. She marries a man who hits her, then dies offscreen so Forrest can raise their son as a saintly single father, conveniently absolving the movie of ever reckoning with her life. She isn't tragic. She's a plot device with a tragic wig. Strip away the soundtrack and the CGI history lessons and nothing remains — no ideas, no edge, no honesty. It's nostalgia sold to people who mistake it for depth. Three hours of comfort food that left a generation convinced it had watched art.

Mon premier visionnage du grand classique Forrest Gump et qu’est-ce que c’est décevant. Le film est une comédie où on place un handicapé dans des situations historiques à travers les décennies 1950 à 1980 et on en rigole. Ça continue pendant 2h30 sans style et sans mise en scène. Les deux seuls personnages avec de vrais arc narratifs sont celui de Jenny qui reste confus et celui de Dan qui est plutôt émouvant. Quant à Forrest, on lui donne ses moments héroïques et touchants, mais tout est en vain dû à la banalité et à la simplicité du scénario. C’est censé être une comédie et ça fait longtemps que je n’ai pas vu une comédie avec si peu d’idées. 90 % des blagues sont soit “fish out of the water” (Forrest qui dit à JFK qu’il doit faire du pipi) soit un narrateur peu fiable mais sincère (Forrest qui pense qu'Apple est une entreprise qui vend des fruits). Tout au long du film, on balance ces deux blagues sans cesse. C’est fatigant et déplacé vu que les rigolades sont basées sur le fait que Forrest soit handicapé. Après 20 minutes, je me disais “ils ne peuvent pas continuer à se moquer de Forrest en le représentant comme ‘débile’ pendant 2h30”, mais tristement j’avais tort. À part les prétendues vannes, les dialogues ne font qu'avancer l'intrigue et vomir des maximes. Tout est mécanique et sans profondeur. Il faut noter aussi que les accents du Sud des États-Unis sont terriblement maladroits. Je n’en pouvais plus de Hanks et de Wright après 20 minutes. Je ne sais pas si je donnerai une autre chance à Forrest Gump dans l’avenir, peut-être pour Lieutenant Dan, mais je trouve ça choquant à quel point le film a mal vieilli.

I'm really conflicted about this movie. It's either a 4d chess move satire or just chocolate covered US propaganda and I can't see which it is. We get 3 main characters in the movie, Forrest, Jenny and Lieutantent Dan. Each have their own arc and as this movie heavily implies, destiny. Dan loves his country, is willing to die for it, does his best, and after sacrificing his legs, he gets tossed aside by society and would have died in poverty and agony if not for Forrest. He on the other hand has been dealt the worst cards. He is dumb with an IQ of 75, but quickly realising that he has no agency of his life anyway. He it too dumb to think and just does as he is told. Never making a decision on his own behalf and look at that. A football player in high school, a war hero, a billionaire, a pop icon and in the end even gets the girl he loves and has a family. And lastly we get the tragic character of the story, Jenny. Jenny is what we now would call woke. She cares about social issues. Makes her voice known and uses her privilege to change the world she lives in. And what does she get in return? She gets abused, becomes an addict and in the end dies of aids. Her whole arc of loving Forrest also just feels as a last desperate act to save herself when we remove the rose tinted glasses our narrator has on. Her destiny is a clear signal though. Rebel, question the current order? You gonna suffer, have a miserable life and die in agony. Jenny and Forrest pain a clear picture in my head for what this movie wants to say, but Dan is the confusing part. Is it just criticism on the military or a sign that this whole movie criticises the status quo. The fact that we do get punished for wanting justice and equality. Nevertheless, most people love this movie, seeing it as a simple story about a guy that with preserverence got rich and famous and leads a great life. Even though he was dealt a horrible hand at birth. A true American dream life. Sadly that message and its rose painted view of life as a string of happy little accidents is very far away from mine. The movie is well shot, well acted and has an amazing soundtrack, but it's message is just really confusing and downright dangerous

Forrest Gump. A name larger and sweeter in the box of chocolates that is the canon of film than just about any of them. You never know what you're gonna get though I guess, and what I once considered my favourite film of all time(!!) when I was maybe 8? 9? has fallen considerably. Maybe movies are like fresh bread: delicious when just baked, but stale and hard to consume when left on the shelf. Pardon that terrible opening paragraph, but it's exactly these kind of schmaltzy, hokey, ridiculous similes that endeared audiences to the titular "dimwitted but loveable" protagonist, and in 2026 I just cannot see why. Forrest's idiosyncratic observations begin likeable enough, but become grating as the film proves time and time again it has no problem punching down on him by giving him everything through sheer chance. This isn't Slumdog Millionaire, there's no pre-ordained destiny for one special person who had agency throughout his life, this is Forrest following orders down the path of least resistance and getting everything. It's a boring, unrealistic fantasy. I recognize a lot of this is played for laughs. Forrest having his money put into 1980s Apple stock by chance or teaching Elvis how to dance by chance or meeting like every president by chance. It's so heightened that I can't get behind it also being simultaneously tear-jerking. You ever cried for Superman? Couldn't be me in my late twenties that's for sure. Was not overly moved by anything Forrest did. Lieutenant Dan is a genuinely sympathetic mentor/enemy/friend. Jenny in contrast to Forrest is a captivating foil, and by far my favourite character, but that's where the politics of Forrest Gump has to be discussed. I heard this was a bit of a boomer pipe dream before going back in, and at minimum I have to agree that it hosts conservative ideals that hinder these character's growth. Obedience to social norms is rewarded (Forrest); resistance is punished (Jenny). The film revels in "heroic" American patriotism and treats resistance groups to the populist ideal as caricatures. Some painfully transparent examples of this being the tone of the scenes featuring the KKK (silly, HAHA Forrest doesn't know the KKK!) in comparison to the Black Panthers (serious, broooo I'm just tryna talk to Jenny why are you all harshing the viiiibe). Jenny isn't given the full villain treatment in my eyes, she's a traumatized child who never finds comfort or stasis, but that empathetic lens is maybe more of mine and less the filmmakers. It's DEFINITELY not heartfelt, and that's what Forrest Gump is best remembered for. It's been over fifteen years since I last watched Forrest Gump. I don't consider it a favourite anymore, not even close, but I'd rather have a change of heart for this film than remain ignorant and naive to who this film represents: the ignorant and naive.

Forrest Gump, c'est le genre de gars, même si tu utilises la technique des écouteurs, il continuera de parler. Un scénario centré sur l'existence , le sens de notre vie , à travers le récit et le monologue de ce personnage. Qui se démarque particulièrement. En effet, Forrest Gump est un personnage présenté comme étant naïf, ainsi, il ne cherche pas une certaine gloire ou richesse, ni même à donner un sens précis aux événements tragiques ou historiques qu'il traverse tout au long de sa vie. Il suit le cours du vent selon ses sentiments, ses convictions et ce qu'il juge bon à ses yeux. À l'inverse de Jenny , une femme instable, qui traverse plusieurs choses afin de trouver sa place dans la vie, de se trouver une raison de vivre, d'où le fait qu'elle passe son temps à partir, revenir, voyager. Ce qui oppose les deux personnages et leur amour : est-ce possible quand l'un ne cherche pas réellement à définir qui il est, et que l'autre est bornée à fuir son passé et à trouver un sens à tout ça ? Ainsi, on pourrait interpréter l'existence dans cette vie comme étant le hasard , où l'on se retrouve là au bon moment, ou bien le destin , où l'on fait des choix ou l'on vit des choses parce que c'est écrit quelque part, comme le pense Dan . Ça montre aussi qu'aux yeux de la société, si t'es jugé comme étant un individu « différent » , d'entrée de jeu, cela suffit à déterminer que tu n'as aucun avenir concret dans ce monde. Démontré par Forrest Gump , car malgré sa simplicité à vivre dans le monde et son QI plus bas que la norme, il a surmonté bien des événements : la guerre, le deuil, se faire des dollars grâce à son entreprise de crevettes et devenir un joueur de ping-pong international... Alors, au final, faut-il courir sans raison et laisser les choses venir à nous ? Ou faire des choix car, de toute façon, c'est ce qui est prédestiné pour nous ? Il est vrai que le message transmis par ce film peut affecter notre perception de la vie. Mais je dois avouer que je me sentais lâcher le fil à cause de la lenteur du récit (je ne dis pas qu'il fallait mettre les turbos, au contraire, ça va très bien avec le contexte : être sur un banc et entendre un individu raconter sa vie sans lui avoir demandé quoi que ce soit...). Et bien que ce que raconte Forrest Gump soit particulièrement captivant (il a eu une vie bien remplie) , je pense que ce n'est pas quelque chose qui me parle. Je ne vous mentirai pas. Forrest drinks fifteen Dr Peppers before meeting Kennedy, which is the nearest this film comes to an honest account of American opportunity. A man has been invited into the White House on the strength of his football and discovers that refreshments are free. Naturally he behaves like somebody who has never been told the price of anything in Washington. When Kennedy asks how he feels, Forrest has to urinate. Zemeckis presumably intended a charming collision between innocence and public history. I was more interested in the presidential catering arrangement, whose principal beneficiaries appear to be those already invited inside. His bladder, at least, is answerable to material conditions.

I appear to be one of the few people on the planet who was not entirely bowled over by the cultural phenomenon that was, and perhaps still is, Forrest Gump. While the movie undoubtedly has its charms, and Tom Hanks et al turn in good performances, I just don't think that it was ever that interesting a story. Obviously it has fantastical elements that require a suspension of disbelief, and maybe this all taps into some kind of nostalgia felt by his fellow Americans for a different era where things were more simple (er, like the Vietnam War?) but Forrest Gump is too unlikely and simplistic an individual, full of contrasting character traits, for me to understand why so many were enchanted by his personal odyssey. Would the movie succeed so well if it were released in these more cynical times? Somehow I suspect not.

I know Forrest Gump is considered one of the greatest films of all time, and I can appreciate why so many people love it, but honestly, it just didn't do much for me. Tom Hanks gives a good performance, and there's no denying the film has some memorable moments, but I found the whole storyline a bit hard to connect with. The film follows Forrest through several decades of American history, with him somehow finding himself involved in all sorts of major events along the way. There's certainly an interesting concept behind it, and some of the moments are quite clever, but I struggled to get invested in the story. It jumps between different stages of his life, and while there's plenty happening, I never really found myself particularly drawn into it. I also found the film a little too sentimental at times, and I think a lot of its emotional moments just didn't land with me the way they're intended to. I can appreciate the messages about love, friendship, loyalty and making the most of life, but it felt like something was missing for me. It's clearly a well-made film with a great soundtrack and a strong performance from Tom Hanks, and I understand why it's so highly regarded. It just wasn't my cup of tea. Sometimes a film can be critically acclaimed and loved by just about everyone, but that doesn't mean it's going to click with you. This was one of those films for me.

Dude deserved literally anyone other than Jenny. This is not the classic I’ve heard so much about. Everything is painfully staged to be whimsically wholesome/life affirming that it’s borderline a parody of the genre. Doesn’t help that Forrest isn’t even that interesting as a character and the major historical milestones he goes through are inconsequential to his life. He barely leaves an impact on the people he meets and the movie wants you to think his small contribution made a difference when he was a footnote in their lives. On top of this is one of the most forced romances I’ve ever seen that is so emotionally bankrupt that all the revelations about it fall completely flat. It’s an emotionally manipulative film that may have convinced everyone else it’s good, but not me. The runners who followed have a long way back.

He visto esta película mil veces, pero a raíz de algunas reviews he decidido observarla de forma más crítica y no en modo automático, como cuando era crío. Aunque se presenta como la típica historia de la inocencia del bobalicón frente a la maldad y la locura del mundo, creo que en el fondo es una suerte de fantasía que enarbola al hombre de bien americano. Forrest no cuestiona nada, simplemente obedece, cumple con su deber y sigue adelante. La convulsa historia de su país es caricaturizada y queda reducida a un decorado por el que él transita sin demasiadas preguntas. Al final, se trata de una oda bastante conservadora a la meritocracia: haz lo que se espera de ti, sé buena persona y la providencia, de una forma u otra, terminará recompensándote. Mientras, Jenny, no solo es reducida a víctima pasiva, sino que además es continuamente ridículizada y castigada por cuestionarse su mundo o vivir en sus márgenes.
